meta.title: MicroPython on Pi Pico
meta.caveat: Initial pass covering only chapters 5-6 (the first two converted chapters with a real assignment/project). A fuller realignment across all 12 chapters is planned once the rest are converted.

alignment_log.scope: First pass: chapters 5 (traffic light controller) and 6 (reaction game) against all four frameworks
alignment_log.note: Initial alignment; nothing re-checked yet since this is the carrier's first version.

1.2.note: Chapter 5's pedestrian-crossing button and chapter 6's two-player buttons both use a hardware interrupt (machine.Pin.irq) to run code in response to a real-world trigger rather than in a fixed top-to-bottom order -- the textbook event-driven case this topic covers.

3.16.note: The traffic light program models a real intersection's light cycle: a simplified stand-in with its own state (which light is on) that updates over time, built for the specific purpose of demonstrating control logic rather than modeling every detail of a real signal.

3.15.note: random.uniform(5, 10) picks how long the LED stays lit before the player can react, so a player can't just count down a fixed number of seconds -- a direct use of a random value drawn from a range.

3.1.note: Both chapters rely on a global variable (button_pressed in chapter 5, fastest_btn in chapter 6) that the main program reads and an interrupt handler writes, so its value has to be reasoned about across two separate points of execution.

3.8.note: The traffic light cycle itself is a straightforward while True loop; the lesson doesn't dig into loop termination conditions or nested iteration beyond that one repeating cycle.

3.13.note: One handler function (btn_handler) serves both the left and right buttons in the two-player version -- the same procedure runs for either input, distinguished only by the pin parameter it's called with, exactly the one-procedure-many-inputs idea this topic covers.

3.6.note: The two-player version decides a winner with if fastest_btn is left_btn / elif fastest_btn is right_btn -- straightforward conditionals, though comparing object identity rather than a value is a slightly different angle than the topic's own examples.

9-12.AP.15.note: Both chapters replace straight-line, run-to-completion code with a button press (an event) that changes what runs next via an interrupt handler -- the standard's own framing almost verbatim.

9-12.AP.14.note: Chapter 5 contrasts polling (checking a button in the main loop) with using an interrupt, and picks the interrupt for a reason it gives -- a real control-structure choice, though the lesson doesn't have students weigh the tradeoff themselves.

9-12.CS.3.note: Wiring three LEDs, a button, and a buzzer to the right pins on a breadboard is exactly the kind of troubleshooting-by-testing this standard describes, but the lesson doesn't frame it as a debugging skill explicitly.

9-12.DA.11.note: The lesson states a real baseline (average human reaction time, ~200-250ms) that a player's own measured result can be compared against, but it doesn't ask students to use the comparison to adjust a model.

S1-PHY-HC-01.note: Both chapters have students build a working circuit from a wiring diagram and figure out why it doesn't work when a wire or pin is wrong -- this standard's own example (an LED that won't light) almost exactly.

S1-PHY-IO-02.note: The pedestrian-crossing button triggering the buzzer is the standard's own example verbatim -- a button triggering a buzzer -- wired and coded so the system reacts to a real button press.

HS-ALG-PS-04.note: The single-player game's use of random.uniform(5, 10) means the same program gives a different light-up delay every run, the exact contrast this standard draws between deterministic and randomness-driven algorithms.

S1-GMD-DD-03.note: The reaction game is a small, complete game: input (a button press) that does something (stops the timer), and rules (whichever pin triggered first) that decide the outcome.

HS-PRO-RD-17.note: Both programs can be read by tracing what the shared variable holds, what the loop repeats, and what the conditional branches on -- though neither lesson asks students to explain this explicitly themselves.

C4.5.note: Both chapters are a hands-on example of the event-driven paradigm this standard names, in contrast to the purely procedural style of earlier chapters.

C9.5.note: Both projects are a microcontroller (the Pico) programmed to run a physical device -- a traffic light system and a reaction-time game -- the standard's own example.

C4.9.note: Chapter 6 exercises the full toolkit this standard names in one lesson: branches and loops, a reusable procedure that takes a parameter, and variables holding state across calls.

C9.3.note: The button-to-interrupt-to-LED/buzzer chain is hardware capturing input, processing it, and acting on it, though the lesson doesn't frame it in those terms.

5.5.note: Debugging a miswired breadboard circuit takes the same structured, methodical approach this standard describes, though the lesson doesn't teach the approach itself, just requires it.

5.12.note: The winner-decision logic is boolean comparisons (is left_btn / is right_btn), though the lesson doesn't discuss boolean logic as a topic in its own right.
